observations:
Torah #196 contains six concepts distributed across two packages. No cluster of 3+ concepts was found that forms an independent bechina domain unaccounted for by the two identified packages.

The teaching's entire bechina content resolves into two clear families:
(1) The evil posture of prayer — תפלת קבע / גזלה / להתעקש בתפלתו / לוקח דבר בחזקה (Package 1)
(2) The good posture of prayer — תפלה / רחמים ותחנונים (Package 2)

These are not sub-domains within a larger thematic universe; they are the totality of the Torah's bechina structure. The teaching operates on a single conceptual axis — the polarity between proper-prayer (supplication) and sinful-prayer (demand) — and uses only one bechina equivalence to make its point: keva = robbery.

No independent domain with 3+ concepts was found that is both:
(a) Connected by bechina (parallel-nature) edges — NOT merely cause-effect, and
(b) Conceptually distinct from Packages 1 and 2.

Candidate examined and rejected — 'Earthly Needs' cluster (פרנסה, בנים, שאר צרכים):
The three items listed in line 5 (livelihood, children, other needs) appear as examples of the types of prayer requests, not as bechina-identified concepts forming their own domain. The Rebbe's structure is: 'whatever you ask — whether X or Y or Z — the rule applies equally.' This is an enumeration of the scope of the eitza (the instruction applies to all prayer), not a bechina identification of X, Y, Z as sharing a special parallel nature distinct from prayer itself. The three items are grammatically objects of the verb 'to request,' not bechina-equals of each other or of any other concept. A 'needs cluster' package would be built on eitza relationships (prayer for parnasah → parnasah) rather than bechina, which violates the framework rule that packages are built on bechina only.

Conclusion: Torah #196's two packages (תפלת קבע וגזלה / תפלה ברחמים ותחנונים) fully exhaust the bechina graph for this Torah. The teaching is conceptually complete with minimal bechina content — a deliberate economy that reflects its nature as a brief, focused mussar instruction rather than an expansive kabbalistic exposition.
